subtype: Processions and ceremonial movement [Interpreting]
passage:
Dear Trisha,

You would have loved last Saturday. I was walking back from the library when a wedding baraat came down our street: a white horse and drummers, cousins dancing so hard their turbans slipped, and a small girl on someone's shoulders throwing petals. I stopped at the kerb. To me it looked like pure joy, but the woman beside me said quietly that the groom's grandmother had died last year and this was the first celebration since. So for her the noise also held a little missing. I don't know the family, so I just clapped when they passed and stayed out of the way. I'm still thinking about how one procession can say two things.

Write soon.
Ojas

qa.q: What did the small girl throw as the baraat passed?
qa.a: She threw petals from someone's shoulders.

qa.q: What was Ojas feeling as Ojas watched the baraat, and how did the woman's remark complicate it?
qa.a: To Ojas it looked like pure joy, and the woman added that it was the first celebration since the groom's grandmother died, so it also held a little missing.

qa.q: How could Ojas respectfully learn more about what a procession means?
qa.a: Ojas could observe from the side, stay out of the way, and ask someone from the family or community what it means to them.

qa.q: How might the groom's family feel about the procession compared with a passer-by?
qa.a: The family may feel joy and loss together, while a passer-by like Ojas may see only the celebration.

grounding: Ojas reads a wedding procession as joy and learns from a bystander that it also carries loss.

subtype: Processions and ceremonial movement [Interpreting]
passage: So I'm Saurabh, and I was on exchange in Edinburgh when I first stood on the pavement watching a graduation march. Hundreds of students in black gowns and coloured hoods walked slowly behind a piper, and I assumed it was pure celebration. Then my flatmate Chetan, who'd graduated the year before, said, "Look at their faces. Some are happy and some are relieved, and the ones near the back are thinking about who couldn't be here." I hadn't thought of that. I asked him what the hoods meant and he said each colour showed a subject. I kept quiet as they passed. I realised the walk felt solemn to them, not just festive, and I'd only have known by asking.

qa.q: Which city was Saurabh in on exchange?
qa.a: Saurabh was on exchange in Edinburgh.

qa.q: What was Saurabh feeling about the march at first, and how did Chetan's remark change that view?
qa.a: Saurabh assumed it was pure celebration, and Chetan added that some students look happy, some relieved, and some are thinking about people who couldn't be there.

qa.a: Saurabh could ask people who took part what the march and hoods mean to them and observe respectfully.

qa.q: How might a graduate see the slow walk behind the piper?
qa.a: It may feel solemn and meaningful to them, marking an end and a beginning, more than just a party.

grounding: Saurabh reads a graduation march as celebration and learns from a friend that it carries solemn meanings too.

subtype: Public demonstrations and peaceful protest [Expressing]
passage:
Dear Deepika,

I joined the water-rights march on Sunday, and I want to tell you how it felt. We gathered at the park gate and walked together to the town hall, chanting a line the organisers gave us. It was surprising how quiet I felt inside. My legs were shaky at first, but the calm of the crowd carried me. Before we started, I noted the two exits, kept my phone charged, and stayed near the marshals with bright bands. When the crowd got tight near the main road, I stepped to the side. I'm glad I went. It felt good to say something with my body, not just my posts. Come next time, if you want.

Trisha

qa.q: Where did the marchers gather?
qa.a: They gathered at the park gate.

qa.q: What did Trisha feel during the march, and what helped Trisha?
qa.a: Trisha felt quiet inside after being shaky at first, and the calm of the crowd carried Trisha along.

qa.q: What safety steps did Trisha take that a wise person might copy?
qa.a: Trisha noted the exits, kept the phone charged, stayed near the marshals and stepped aside when the crowd got tight.

qa.q: How might Deepika feel reading Trisha's invitation?
qa.a: Deepika may feel curious and a little cautious, since Trisha describes both the calm and the precautions Trisha took. 🙂

grounding: Trisha joins a peaceful march to voice a concern and stays aware of safety and exits.

Our chant was simple, and our teacher, Minakshi, had told us to keep it peaceful and to check with the police about where we could stand. My heart was thumping. I looked at the girl next to me, and she squeezed my arm. Before we began I found the gate we'd use to leave if it got crowded. Nothing bad happened. An officer took our letter and said it would go up. I don't know whether it will change anything, but I felt heard for the first time.

subtype: Grateful, welcoming and joyful in new communities [Interpreting]

On the third evening, a girl I'd only nodded to knocked and handed me a laddoo, saying, "It's my sister's engagement, so everyone gets one." I nearly said "no thanks" out of shyness. I took it. Later Kamal from the next room asked if I wanted to join their group for chai. I said yes, then panicked, then went. Afterwards I texted my mother that people here were kind. It felt like I'd been counted in, in a very small way. I said thank you three times, which they laughed about.

She'd planned a proper dinner for Amandeep's birthday, but the day had gone wrong. Instead, she sat on the edge of the bed and wrote on a sticky note: "Dal is in the red box, put it on low. Don't wait up. Saturday, just us, your choice." Amandeep, coming home soaked, read it at the door and grinned. He had wanted her to call, but this was her way: things done, plans made. He made tea, put a note back in her bag that read "Hope the night is quiet", and ran to find her an umbrella.

passage: Anand admired his lab mentor, Dr. Rao, and had been trying to say so for months. Every Wednesday he stayed after class to ask a question about her methods and took notes as she answered. His girlfriend, Disha, waited in the corridor, scrolling her phone, and said one evening, "You talk about her more than you talk about us." Anand paused. "I don't mean to. Learning from her is how I show I admire someone." Disha nodded slowly. "And I like being taken to dinner, or getting a message at lunch." They stood there, both a little embarrassed. Anand said, "Tell me what feels like care. I don't want to guess." She smiled. "Lunch messages. Start there."

grounding: Anand shows admiration by learning from a mentor and asks Disha what feels caring.

subtype: Grieving and sorrowful away from home [Regulating]
passage: Sunday night, 11 pm. Papa called this morning to say Nani had died in her sleep. I'm in Pune. The funeral was today, and I couldn't get a train in time. I said I was fine on the phone. I said it twice. Then I went to my room and looked at her photo on my shelf for an hour. I'm Neelam, and this is the first time I've written a diary in months. My roommate Swati came in with tea and didn't ask anything. She sat on the floor. I told her about Nani's mango pickle and started to cry. I lit a small lamp by the photo. Tomorrow I'll call Papa again and ask him about her last days. I think I want to ask the college counsellor too.

qa.a: Swati did not ask questions and just sat with Neelam, so Neelam could speak about Nani when ready.

grounding: Neelam grieves far from home, puts on a brave face, then reaches out, marks the loss and thinks of a counsellor.

Instead I said, "I need to step out for a few minutes," and I walked to the corridor and counted my breaths by the window. When I came back, I said, "Can we agree on a time for your section? Tomorrow at noon?" He nodded. His reply was quieter than usual, and I don't know if he was embarrassed or annoyed. Either way, we now have a time. He crossed to a brightly lit takeaway, went in and stood near the counter. The man walked on. Javier texted Chen, "Can you meet me here? Feeling a bit weird." Chen arrived in ten minutes and they walked home together. Javier told the shop worker thanks. He decided to mention it to the campus security in the morning, in case others noticed the same thing.

Tushar nodded, said "that sounds awful" and didn't offer a plan. I watched him pass her a tissue. After about fifteen minutes she said she was thinking of seeing her professor, and he offered to walk her to the office. I can't say how she felt, but she stood up straighter.

subtype: Skeptical and questioning in learning [Regulating]

Day three. Chetan looked up the claim. The post cited no study and the writer sold the tea. He told Leela, a little sheepish, that he'd nearly forwarded it.

Day eight. Another post arrived. This time Chetan asked three things before sharing: who says it, what evidence, and who gains. Leela nodded. He also caught himself thinking that nothing online could be trusted, and stopped. Some sources were fine. He just had to check.

grounding: Chetan learns to question a source fairly over several days without tipping into cynicism.

subtype: Skeptical and questioning in learning [Regulating]
passage: I'm Kunal, and I have been a journalist for forty years. Let me tell you about Bhavna, my intern back then. She was twenty and could not let a claim pass. A politician's aide gave us a number about the town's water supply, and everyone else copied it. Bhavna asked, "Where does the number come from, and how was it counted?" It irritated the aide and half the newsroom. But she was polite about it, and she was curious, not smug. It turned out the number was from a different year. She wasn't cynical, mind you. When the second source checked out, she happily used it. That's the difference I'd like you to remember: doubt that wants to find out, not doubt that wants to win.

qa.q: How old was Bhavna as an intern?
qa.a: She was twenty.

qa.q: What made Bhavna's questioning fair and useful, according to Kunal?

qa.q: What could a young reader take from Bhavna's example?

grounding: An elder recalls Bhavna's fair, curious questioning of a claim, distinguishing it from cynicism.
